card.headline: Never give up synonyms
card.sub: 20 other ways to say it, from casual to formal

beats.copied_from: open loop: BBC 6 Minute English Tcf1dbiWKsk (question at the start, answer later) + Daily English Talk 1fpTA_SuRuY ('we will tell you at the very end')
beats.speech: Never give up synonyms: here are twenty other ways to say never give up, from what you text a friend to what you write in a job application. But be careful. One word on many never give up lists is actually an insult. Which one? You'll find out in part four.

beats.label: say it to a friend
beats.chapter: Say it to a friend: keep going, hang in there

card.headline: Say it to a friend
card.sub: Part 1 of 4 · everyday English

beats.speech: Part one. Five things you say to a friend who wants to quit, or to yourself.
beats.revised: 2026-10-18 critic fix 2: B2 (13 s empty card) cut, its 'or to yourself' folded in here

card.headline: Keep going
card.meaning: continue, even when it's hard
card.example: You're halfway there. Keep going!

beats.speech: Keep going. It means continue, even when it's hard. You're halfway there. Keep going!

card.headline: Hang in there
card.meaning: don't give up while things are hard (informal)
card.example: I know this week is awful. Hang in there.

beats.speech: Hang in there. It's informal, and it means don't give up while things are hard. I know this week is awful. Hang in there.

card.headline: Keep at it
card.meaning: keep working at something difficult
card.example: Your English is getting better. Keep at it!

beats.speech: Keep at it. It means keep working at something difficult. Your English is getting better. Keep at it!

card.headline: Stick with it
card.meaning: don't stop, even when it gets boring or hard
card.example: The first month is the hardest. Stick with it.

beats.speech: Stick with it. It means don't stop, even when it gets boring or hard. The first month is the hardest. Stick with it.

card.headline: You've got this
card.meaning: you can do it (very informal)
card.example: Big interview tomorrow? You've got this.

beats.speech: You've got this. It means you can do it, and it's very informal. Big interview tomorrow? You've got this.

card.headline: Which one fits?
card.question: Third driving test failed? ___ You'll pass next time.
card.answer: Third driving test failed? Hang in there. You'll pass next time.

beats.speech: Your friend has just failed her driving test for the third time. What do you say? Hang in there, or congratulations? | Hang in there. Congratulations would sound sarcastic here.

card.headline: Which one fits?
card.question: Your English is getting better. Keep ___ it!
card.answer: Your English is getting better. Keep at it!

beats.speech: Your English is getting better. Which is right: keep at it, or keep with it? | Keep at it. But we say stick with it.
beats.revised: 2026-10-18 critic fix 5: spoken 'keep blank it' was heard as 'keep blanket'

card.headline: Say it with me
card.sentences:
You're halfway there. Keep going!
I know this week is awful. Hang in there.
Your English is getting better. Keep at it!
The first month is the hardest. Stick with it.
Big interview tomorrow? You've got this.

beats.speech: Now say them out loud with me. Short ones, I promise. | You're halfway there. Keep going! | I know this week is awful. Hang in there. | Your English is getting better. Keep at it! | The first month is the hardest. Stick with it. | Big interview tomorrow? You've got this.

card.headline: He built his own house...
card.sub: ...and this is how it turned out.  One Week (1920), public domain

beats.speech: Look at this man. He built his own house, and this is how it turned out. Crooked. What would you say to him?
beats.copied_from: story of failing and trying again: Daily English Talk 1fpTA_SuRuY (fell off the bike 'maybe the 15th time': 'That's it, I give up'); picture = our public-domain clip library

card.headline: Which one fits?
card.question: He's ready to quit. Tell him: don't throw in the ___!
card.answer: He's ready to quit. Tell him: don't throw in the towel!

beats.speech: Quick guess. He's ready to quit. You tell him: don't throw in the blank. Towel, or hat? | Towel. Don't throw in the towel. More about that in a moment.

card.headline: Then the storm came.
card.sub: This is the moment most people give up.  One Week (1920), public domain

beats.speech: Then a storm came and twisted the whole house. This is the moment most people give up. Part two is about exactly this moment.

beats.label: after a setback
beats.chapter: After a setback: push through, bounce back

card.headline: After a setback
card.sub: Part 2 of 4 · idioms and phrasal verbs

beats.speech: Part two. Five phrases for after a fall.

card.headline: Don't throw in the towel
card.meaning: don't give up (from boxing)
card.example: Don't throw in the towel now. You're nearly there.

beats.speech: Don't throw in the towel. It means don't give up. In boxing, throwing in the towel means stopping the fight. Don't throw in the towel now. You're nearly there.

card.headline: Push through
card.meaning: keep going through something hard or tiring
card.example: I know you're tired. You can push through this.

beats.speech: Push through. It means keep going through something hard or tiring. I know you're tired. You can push through this.

card.headline: Bounce back
card.meaning: recover quickly after a problem
card.example: It was a bad result, but you'll bounce back.

beats.speech: Bounce back. It means recover quickly after a problem. It was a bad result, but you'll bounce back.

card.headline: Pick yourself up
card.meaning: get up again after a failure
card.example: You fell. Now pick yourself up and try again.

beats.speech: Pick yourself up. It means get up again after a failure. You fell. Now pick yourself up and try again.

card.headline: Soldier on
card.meaning: keep going, even when it's hard or unpleasant
card.example: It's not easy, but we'll soldier on.

beats.speech: Soldier on. It means keep going, even when things are hard or unpleasant. It's not easy, but we'll soldier on.

card.headline: Which one fits?
card.question: It was a bad result, but you'll ___ back.
card.answer: It was a bad result, but you'll bounce back.

beats.speech: It was a bad result, but you'll blank back. Bounce, or jump? | You'll bounce back.

card.headline: Which one fits?
card.question: The project is hard, but we'll ___.
card.options: soldier on / throw in the towel
card.answer: The project is hard, but we'll soldier on.

beats.speech: The project is hard, but we'll blank. Soldier on, or throw in the towel? | We'll soldier on.

card.headline: Say it with me
card.sentences:
Don't throw in the towel now.
You can push through this.
You'll bounce back from this.
Pick yourself up and try again.
It's not easy, but we'll soldier on.

beats.speech: Your turn. Say them with me. | Don't throw in the towel now. | You can push through this. | You'll bounce back from this. | Pick yourself up and try again. | It's not easy, but we'll soldier on.

card.headline: After the storm, they get back up.
card.sub: Pick yourself up.  One Week (1920), public domain

beats.speech: Back to our house. After the storm, it's a wreck. But look: they get up off the ground. That's what pick yourself up means.
beats.revised: 2026-10-18 critic fix 4: the house story was never closed; claims only what the clip shows (people get up and stand in front of the twisted house)

card.headline: Wrong: When I feel give up
card.sub: Right: When I feel like giving up

beats.speech: Now a mistake from real comments. Under one popular video, nine comments said: when I feel give up, or when I feel giving up. The natural way is: when I feel like giving up. After feel like, use giving, going, crying, not give, go, cry.
beats.chapter: Mistakes: when I feel like giving up
beats.copied_from: our angle: no competitor teaches it (NLM q3); evidence = 9 comments under Mr. English Channel AKpfup9Hgi4

card.headline: I gave up drinking coffee.
card.sub: not: I gave up to drink coffee

beats.speech: Give up works the same way: I gave up drinking coffee. Not: I gave up to drink coffee.

card.headline: Give up on someone or something
card.sub: Don't give up on your dreams.  I won't give up on you.

beats.speech: With people and hopes, say give up on. I won't give up on you. Don't give up on your dreams.

beats.label: formal words
beats.chapter: More formal words: persevere, determined, resilient

card.headline: More formal words
card.sub: Part 3 of 4 · work, essays, job applications

beats.speech: Part three. Five more formal words, for work, essays and job applications.

card.headline: Persevere
card.meaning: keep trying for a long time, even when it's difficult (formal)
card.example: She persevered and finally passed the exam.

beats.speech: Persevere. It means keep trying for a long time, even when it's difficult. It's formal. She persevered and finally passed the exam.

card.headline: per · se · VERE
card.sub: stress at the end, like severe.  Spelling: per + severe (not perserve)

beats.speech: Persevere has the word severe inside it. Say it with me: severe. Persevere. The stress is on the last part, just like in severe. And the noun: perseverance. The spelling is easy too: per, plus severe.
beats.copied_from: SpeechModification 2DCV_z3pAhc (15,372 views for this one word; 'it does have the word severe in it ... the main stress is on the veer syllable'); comments misspell it 'perserved'

card.headline: Determined
card.meaning: having decided firmly to do something
card.example: He was determined to finish the marathon.

beats.speech: Determined. It means you've decided firmly to do something. He was determined to finish the marathon.

card.headline: Persistent
card.meaning: trying again and again, even when people say no
card.example: She was persistent, and she got the job.

beats.speech: Persistent. It means trying again and again, even when people say no. She was persistent, and she got the job.

card.headline: Tenacious
card.meaning: holding on and not giving up easily
card.example: She's a tenacious reporter who never drops a story.

beats.speech: Tenacious. It means holding on and not giving up easily. She's a tenacious reporter who never drops a story.

card.headline: Resilient
card.meaning: able to recover after something bad happens
card.example: Kids are often more resilient than we think.

beats.speech: Resilient. It means able to recover after something bad happens. Kids are often more resilient than we think.

card.headline: Persevere or resilient?
card.sub: persevere = you keep going.  resilient = you get back up.

beats.speech: Persevere or resilient? People mix them up. Persevere is about keeping going. Resilient is about getting back up after something knocks you down.
beats.copied_from: our angle: no video contrasts them (NLM q3); a viewer under BBC Tcf1dbiWKsk: 'the picture is suggestive of perseverance rather than resilience' (3 likes)

card.headline: Which one fits?
card.question: She ___ and finally passed the exam.
card.answer: She persevered and finally passed the exam.

beats.speech: She blank and finally passed the exam. Persevered, or preserved? | Persevered. Preserve means keep something safe, like food or old buildings.

card.headline: Which one fits?
card.question: I'm ___ resilient. I give up when things get hard.
card.answer: I'm not resilient. I give up when things get hard.
card.note: not + adjective;  no + noun (I'm no expert)

beats.speech: This one is from a real comment. I'm blank resilient. Not, or no? | I'm not resilient. Not goes before an adjective. No goes before a noun, like I'm no expert.

card.headline: Say it with me
card.sentences:
She persevered and finally passed the exam.
He was determined to finish the marathon.
She was persistent, and she got the job.
She's a tenacious reporter.
Kids are often more resilient than we think.

beats.speech: Say them with me. These words are great for job interviews. | She persevered and finally passed the exam. | He was determined to finish the marathon. | She was persistent, and she got the job. | She's a tenacious reporter. | Kids are often more resilient than we think.

card.headline: Say it to someone
card.sub: You're so determined. You'll get there.  ·  You've been so resilient this year.

beats.speech: Most of these words describe a person. You can use them to encourage someone: You're so determined. You'll get there. Or: You've been so resilient this year. I'm proud of you.
beats.revised: 2026-10-18 critic fix 6: 10 of the 20 words describe a person; show how to say them to someone
beats.copied_from: viewer-critic review 2026-10-18 (gap: describing words are not things you say to someone)

beats.label: praise or insult
beats.chapter: Praise or insult? determined vs stubborn

card.headline: Praise or insult?
card.sub: Part 4 of 4 · the trap

beats.speech: Part four. Five words that seem to mean the same thing, but some are praise and some are criticism. One of them is the insult I promised at the start.

card.headline: Dogged
card.meaning: determined to continue, even when it's slow or hard (praise)
card.example: It took dogged determination to finish the degree.

beats.speech: Dogged. It's praise, and it means determined to continue, even when it's slow or hard. It took dogged determination to finish the degree.

card.headline: Resolute
card.meaning: firm and determined (formal, praise)
card.example: She remained resolute despite the criticism.

beats.speech: Resolute. It's formal praise, and it means firm and determined. She remained resolute despite the criticism.

card.headline: Relentless
card.meaning: never stopping (praise for effort, but also: relentless rain)
card.example: Their relentless training paid off.

beats.speech: Relentless. It means never stopping. It's praise for effort, but we also say relentless rain, or relentless pressure. Their relentless training paid off.

card.headline: Stubborn
card.meaning: refusing to change your mind (usually criticism)
card.example: He's too stubborn to ask for directions.

beats.speech: Stubborn. It's usually criticism, and it means refusing to change your mind. He's too stubborn to ask for directions.

card.headline: Obstinate
card.meaning: stubborn in an unreasonable way (an insult if you say it about someone)
card.example: The obstinate child refused to put his shoes on.

beats.speech: Obstinate. And here's our insult. It means stubborn in an unreasonable way. It's on many never give up lists, but if you say it about someone, it's an insult, not praise. The obstinate child refused to put his shoes on.
beats.revised: 2026-10-18 critic fix 7: card now says insult (thumbnail promise ONE IS AN INSULT)

card.headline: I'm determined. You're stubborn.
card.sub: Same behaviour. It depends who is talking.

beats.speech: Here's a little joke in English. I'm determined. You're stubborn. He's obstinate. Same behaviour, three different opinions.
beats.copied_from: 'don't say X, say this instead' contrast: Go Natural English HzkyjNQ6AqY (its 'sounds sarcastic' moment is the most-liked joke in the T02 comments, 9 likes)

card.headline: Which one fits?
card.question: From a job reference: "She is ___ and hard-working."
card.answer: From a job reference: "She is determined and hard-working."

beats.speech: From a job reference: she is blank and hard-working. Stubborn, determined, or obstinate? | Determined. Stubborn and obstinate would be criticism.

card.headline: Say it with me
card.sentences:
It took dogged determination.
She remained resolute.
Their relentless training paid off.
He's too stubborn to ask for directions.
Don't be obstinate. Just say sorry.

beats.speech: Last practice. Say them with me. | It took dogged determination. | She remained resolute. | Their relentless training paid off. | He's too stubborn to ask for directions. | Don't be obstinate. Just say sorry.

card.headline: Skip these three
card.sub: sedulous · pertinacious · inexorable

beats.speech: Skip three words you'll find on old lists, even on our own old page: sedulous and pertinacious are very rare, and inexorable is usually about things, not people.
beats.copied_from: our page fix: page.txt lists them; NLM q3: none of the 13 page words except persist/determined appears in any competitor video

card.headline: Rest, don't quit.
card.sub: A runner stops for water, but stays in the race.

beats.speech: One more thing. Never give up doesn't mean never stop. A runner stops for water, but doesn't leave the race. Rest, don't quit.
beats.chapter: When not to say never give up
beats.copied_from: Mr. English Channel AKpfup9Hgi4 ('rest don't quit, like a runner in a race...')

card.headline: Sometimes, don't say it at all.
card.sub: A friend is sad or exhausted? Try: I'm here for you.

beats.speech: And sometimes never give up is the wrong thing to say. If a friend is sad or exhausted, it can sound like pressure. Try: I'm here for you.

card.headline: Someone encourages you. You say:
card.sub: Thanks, I needed that.  ·  That means a lot.

beats.speech: And when someone says hang in there to you, what do you say back? Thanks, I needed that. Or: that means a lot.
beats.copied_from: viewer question under Bob the Canadian TIKrfdvZdes: 'I don't know how to answer when someone encourages me' - no video answers it

card.headline: I believe in you.
card.sub: Keep at it.

beats.speech: One last phrase, and this one is for you. Learning English takes months, sometimes years, and some days it feels like nothing works. Keep at it. I believe in you.
beats.copied_from: Bob Baker ChVGiyU8JZY: 'I believe in you' is the phrase its viewers quote; its top comments are about needing to hear it (58 and 29 likes)

card.sub: anotherwordfor.net

beats.speech: All twenty phrases, with examples, are on another word for dot net. The link is in the description.

card.sub: Tell us in the comments.  Next: the video on your screen
